title: India Ends Its Four-Year Fuel Price Freeze — and Every Household Will Feel It
excerpt: The ₹3-per-litre hike, triggered by a global crude surge and war in the Middle East, marks the first increase since 2022 and threatens to push inflation higher at the worst possible moment
body:
For four years, Indian motorists enjoyed something rare in a country accustomed to volatile pump prices: stability. On May 15, that era ended. State-run oil marketing companies — Indian Oil Corporation, Bharat Petroleum, and Hindustan Petroleum — raised petrol and diesel prices by ₹3 per litre, with CNG following at ₹2 per kilogram. In Delhi, petrol now costs ₹99.72 per litre; in Mumbai, diesel has breached ₹97.

The timing is no accident. International crude prices have surged more than 50 per cent since February, driven by the escalating conflict between the United States and Iran, fears over the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint, and a drone strike on the UAE's Barakah nuclear plant that rattled markets further. India, which imports roughly 85 per cent of its crude oil, was running out of room to absorb the shock.

## Why Now, and Why It Matters

The freeze had always been a political calculation. With state elections in the rearview mirror and no imminent polls, the government found a window. But the delay came at a cost. Oil marketing companies had been haemorrhaging money — estimated losses exceeding ₹35,000 crore in the last quarter alone — subsidising consumers while global benchmarks raced ahead.

The ₹3 hike, analysts say, barely dents the gap. "This recovers perhaps a quarter of the under-recovery," said an energy sector analyst at ICICI Securities. "If Brent stays above $105, further hikes of ₹5-7 are mathematically inevitable before monsoon season." Wholesale fuel prices had already spiked 32 per cent for petrol and 25 per cent for diesel in the preceding month.

## The Inflation Ripple

India's consumer price inflation was already at a 42-month high of 5.8 per cent in April, driven by food prices. Fuel touches virtually everything in the supply chain. Trucking costs — the backbone of India's goods movement — will rise almost immediately. Ride-hailing platforms like Ola and Uber are expected to add fuel surcharges within days. Auto-rickshaw unions in Delhi and Mumbai have already demanded fare revisions.

For the 80 million households that use LPG cylinders, the pain is compounding. Cooking gas prices had risen twice since January. For farmers heading into the kharif sowing season, higher diesel costs mean costlier tractor operations, irrigation, and transportation to mandis.

The opposition has pounced. Congress leader Bhupesh Baghel called the hike "a betrayal of the common man" and demanded a rollback. The BJP's response has been to point at global factors — not without justification, but the political narrative around fuel pricing has historically proved combustible.

## What the Diaspora Should Watch

For NRIs sending remittances home, the hike has a dual edge. A weaker rupee — which has depreciated 4 per cent against the dollar this year — means remittances stretch further in rupee terms, but that advantage erodes if domestic inflation eats into purchasing power. Families in smaller towns, where alternative fuels are scarce, will feel the squeeze most acutely.

India's fuel pricing mechanism remains opaque by global standards. Unlike European nations that publish daily refinery-gate prices, Indian OMCs adjust rates in a process that blends economics with political expediency. The government has quietly floated the idea of a "fuel price stabilisation fund" modelled on Indonesia's approach, but no concrete proposal has emerged.

## What Comes Next

The deeper question is whether this is a one-off adjustment or the start of a series. The Iran conflict shows no sign of de-escalation. The International Energy Agency warned last week that global spare capacity is at its thinnest since 2008. India's strategic petroleum reserve — roughly 39 million barrels, enough for about 9.5 days of imports — offers scant cushion.

Government advisers have reportedly begun modelling scenarios for further hikes of ₹2 per litre each month through August, calibrated to limit the inflationary impact to 0.3 percentage points per quarter. Whether the political will exists for such gradualism is another matter entirely. In India, fuel prices are never just about fuel.
